title: Harvard scientists detect radio signals from exoplanet outside solar system for the first time
excerpt: It is not alien technology, but a colossal magnetic powerhouse.Harvard astronomers have pinpointed repeating radio bursts to a planet beyond our solar system, unlocking a new frontier in exoplanet observation.
content:
Astronomers have achieved a historic milestone in planetary science by directly detecting radio emissions from an exoplanet outside our solar system for the first time.

The signals, traced to the young gas giant Beta Pictoris b located roughly 63 light-years from Earth, provide direct observational proof of an immense planetary magnetic field. While radio signals in deep space often evoke searches for extraterrestrial intelligence, researchers emphasized that the broadcast is entirely natural—generated by massive auroral storms supercharged by the planet's rotation.

"I know radio signals are associated with searches for extraterrestrial intelligence, but this is something very different," explained Edo Berger, professor of astronomy at Harvard University and senior coauthor of the study, conducted alongside lead author Kevin Ortiz Ceballos at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian.

Key Astronomical Data and Discovery Details

The detection, posted to the preprint server ArXiv ahead of formal peer-reviewed journal publication, relies on high-resolution observations gathered by the MeerKAT radio telescope array in South Africa:

  • Target Exoplanet: Beta Pictoris b, a gas giant with an estimated mass roughly 12 times that of Jupiter.
  • Distance and Host System: Located 63 light-years away in the constellation Pictor, orbiting a young host star 1.75 times more massive than our sun.
  • System Age: Approximately 23 million years old—an infant planetary system compared to our 4.5-billion-year-old solar system.
  • Signal Properties: Repeating, strongly circularly polarized radio bursts detected across frequency bands between 0.85 GHz and 3.5 GHz.
  • Magnetic Field Intensity: Measurements reveal an extraordinary magnetic field strength of at least 1.25 kilogauss—more than 200 times stronger than Jupiter's, which previously held the record for the most powerful planetary magnetic field observed.

Auroral Engines: Why the Planet Emits Radio Waves

The mechanism producing the radio signals mirrors the physical processes that generate the Northern and Southern Lights on Earth, as well as the intense radio emissions observed around Jupiter and Saturn.

When high-energy charged particles become trapped within the magnetic field lines of Beta Pictoris b, they accelerate rapidly along the poles. Through a physical phenomenon known as electron cyclotron maser instability, these spiraling electrons generate intense bursts of coherent radio waves alongside visible and ultraviolet auroras.

On Jupiter, similar auroral emissions are driven by volcanic particles spewed from its moon Io. On Beta Pictoris b, the extreme scale of the planet and its rapid youth generate auroral energy on an unprecedented magnitude, effectively causing the planet's magnetosphere to broadcast high-frequency radio pulses across interstellar space.

Planetary magnetic fields serve as critical shields against destructive stellar winds and cosmic radiation, protecting upper atmospheres from being stripped away. Detecting these fields directly provides researchers with a vital tool to assess atmospheric stability and interior planetary structures on worlds beyond our solar system.

Isolating the Planet from Its Host Star

While astronomers have observed tentative radio signals in other distant systems over recent years, past candidates—such as the red dwarf system YZ Ceti—left lingering doubts about whether the stellar flare activity of the host star was the true culprit.

In this instance, the Harvard-led team successfully resolved the spatial signature of the emission, isolating the radio pulses directly to the orbit of Beta Pictoris b rather than its parent star or surrounding debris disks. Independent astrophysicists noted that observing radio waves at such high frequencies contradicted conventional models, which assumed exoplanetary magnetic fields would produce emissions at much lower frequencies similar to our own gas giants.

The Beta Pictoris system remains one of the most thoroughly investigated in modern astrophysics, home to three confirmed giant planets, dozens of comets, and a massive circumstellar disk of cosmic dust first photographed by astronomers in 1984.

The research team has submitted requests for additional observing time on global radio telescope arrays to track the rotational period of Beta Pictoris b and evaluate whether companion planets in the system exhibit similar magnetic activity.
